# Determinants of system transparency and its influence on trust in and reliance on unmanned robotic systems

Scott Ososky<sup>a</sup>, Tracy Sanders<sup>a</sup>, Florian Jentsch<sup>a</sup>, Peter Hancock<sup>a</sup> & Jessie Y. C. Chen<sup>b a</sup>University of Central Florida, Orlando, FL; b<sub>U</sub>.S. Army Research Laboratory, Orlando, FL

## ABSTRACT

Increasingly autonomous robotic systems are expected to play a vital role in aiding humans in complex and dangerous environments. It is unlikely, however, that such systems will be able to consistently operate with perfect reliability. Even less than 100% reliable systems can provide a significant benefit to humans, but this benefit will depend on a human operator’s ability to understand a robot’s behaviors and states. The notion of system transparency is examined as a vital aspect of robotic design, for maintaining humans’ trust in and reliance on increasingly automated platforms. System transparency is described as the degree to which a system’s action, or the intention of an action, is apparent to human operators and/or observers. While the physical designs of robotic systems have been demonstrated to greatly influence humans’ impressions of robots, determinants of transparency between humans and robots are not solely robot-centric. Our approach considers transparency as emergent property of the human–robot system. In this paper, we present insights from our interdisciplinary efforts to improve the transparency of teams made up of humans and unmanned robots. These nearfuturistic teams are those in which robot agents will autonomously collaborate with humans to achieve task goals. This paper demonstrates how factors such as human–robot communication and human mental models regarding robots impact a human’s ability to recognize the actions or states of an automated system. Furthermore, we will discuss the implications of system transparency on other critical HRI factors such as situation awareness, operator workload, and perceptions of trust.

**Keywords:** human–robot interaction, autonomous systems, transparency, trust, reliability, human–robot teams, mental models, situation awareness

## 1. INTRODUCTION

Human reliance on robots in complex and dangerous environments is expected to continue expanding. This is due to both ongoing technological advancements in artificial intelligence and sensing capabilities, and the obvious benefits that robots already provide in keeping humans out of harm’s way. This trend is, perhaps, most readily evidenced by the recent news that the US Army is considering downsizing the human contingent of its forces by as many as 80,000 Soldiers over the next five years [1]. In order to compensate for the reduction in manpower due to the re-scoping of defense budgets, as well as to support the continuing evaluation of the strategic/operational environment, the US military is looking to robotic systems to partner with and augment the capabilities of Soldiers. This approach is further detailed in the most recent iteration of the US Department of Defense Unmanned Systems Integrated Roadmap, which spans FY2013 to 2038 [2]. This roadmap describes R&D efforts in the near and future term to advance the capabilities of unmanned robotic assets in ground, sea, and air applications. However, in order to realize the benefits that advanced autonomous robots may provide, there are unique challenges that collaborative robotics must first address, including trust and transparency in robotic teammates.

Of particular relevance to the current discussion is the advancement of autonomous capabilities in unmanned ground systems, specifically within the military domain. Increased autonomy in ground robots provides a pathway from tools to teammates [3], positioning robots as collaborating members of teams that consist of human and robotic members. However, it is not expected (or perhaps even desirable) that the autonomous capabilities of robots will replicate the capabilities of their human counterparts [4]. Rather, collaborative robotics presents an opportunity to develop systems that complement the strengths and weaknesses of human teammates. Likewise, humans can compensate for the limitations of robotic systems through bi-directional communication channels during task execution. Robots, therefore, do not need to be 100% reliable in order for them to be useful, but it is critical that humans place an appropriate amount of trust in, and reliance on robotic systems to effectively leverage their capabilities [5]. Trust can be properly calibrated given an accurate understanding of the outputs and likely failures of a robotic system, as well as the factors that may lead to those outcomes. The notion of system transparency is a means through which humans and robots can arrive at the shared understanding required for trust, however the transparency construct is not as clear as its name may suggest. For instance, can a robotic system be considered transparent if a human teammate cannot detect transparency-relevant signals from a robot? What is the impact on human–robot teamwork if signals from the robot are interpreted incorrectly? We submit that system transparency, within the domain of collaborative robotics, is not solely a characteristic or feature of a robotic asset; rather, it is an emergent characteristic of the human–robot system.

The purpose of this document, then, is to explore the influence of system transparency on human-robot interaction (HRI). We begin with an overview of the system transparency concept, as well as how the transition in the robot’s system-role from a teleoperated tool to a collaborating teammate affects the operationalization of transparency in human–robot systems. We leverage insights from three parallel, related interdisciplinary research efforts to illustrate the relationship of transparency to other critical constructs in HRI, including mental models, situation awareness, and trust. Suggestions and guidance are offered throughout in support of the effort to integrate transparency into the ongoing development of autonomous unmanned ground robots, as well as the human–robot system as a whole.

## 1.1. System transparency

In general, something is described as transparent when it is “able to be seen through” or “easy to notice or understand” [6]. While these two definitions are similar in explanation, they are functionally quite different. Indeed, the concept of transparency, applied to human-system interaction, can also be operationalized in one of these two functionally distinct categories, based around the notions of seeing through and seeing into, respectively.

The first interpretation of system transparency, in which the system is seen through, or invisible to the user, is exemplified by the modern web-browser. Browsers on computers, tablets, and smartphones are trending toward a minimalistic interface. Compared with earlier generations of browsers, the UI of modern web browsers have fewer toolbars, buttons, and input boxes. One purpose of this design is to make the browser interface transparent, or more invisible, to the user, thus allowing the user to feel as if they are interacting with the UI of the web pages (not the browser) directly. To that end, many desktop browsers now offer a full screen mode where the browser UI disappears completely. A similar interpretation of system transparency has been identified as critical to remote manipulation and teleoperation of robotic systems. For instance, Raju and colleagues [7] described a property of an ideal telemanipulator as one “that provides complete transparency of the interface … the operator feels as if the task object were being handled directly” (p. 1318). Applying this to tele-medicine, Troccaz and colleagues [8] stated that transparency in a remote surgery system “has to be as good as possible” (p. 731), meaning that the remote system has minimal input delay and does not impede the physical capabilities of the surgeon themselves. Further, the transparency of these types of tele-present systems might actually be increased with the inclusion of feedback mechanisms (force, vibration, etc.), which simulate the forces a user would feel when manipulating an object directly [9].

The second example of transparency of interest to HRI is concerned with revealing information to the user and supplementing expected outputs, which reveal how a system works and/or what it is doing. Consider the following descriptions of system transparency from the HCI literature: “when a user can immediately understand what the system is doing, and how, by viewing the interface” (p.61) [10] and “easy-to-understand and intuitive” (p. 118) [11]. The common theme in these descriptions of transparency is the support of user understanding. An accessible example of this type of transparency is seen in recommendation systems, such as those found within Netflix and Amazon. Recommendation systems examine user behavior (e.g., watching, buying, browsing) in order to make intelligent suggestions to the user regarding other items in which they might be interested. Transparency manifests in these systems where the UI offers a justification for the recommendation (e.g., “You might be interested in product X, based on your recent purchase of product Y,” or “People who bought Y also purchased X”). While revealing the details of the decision logic to the user does not alter the recommendation output itself, there is evidence to suggest that the user’s experience with and perception of the system is positively influenced by system transparency, including positive associations with trust and users’ willingness to continue interacting with the system [12].

## 1.2. Transparency from tools to teammates

The distinction between these two types of system transparency is also characteristic of the transition in military ground robotic systems from tools to teammates (or, from teleloperation to collaboration). Where teleoperated robots are deployed, elements of transparency that pertain to invisibility are often desirable (e.g., low response latency, haptic feedback in remote manipulation of objects). These types of transparency features are those that encourage situation awareness (SA) of the remote environment, but not necessarily SA of the remote system itself. It is important to note however, that due to number of potential ways in which ground robots can fail in the field [13], complete system transparency/invisibility, while desirable, is typically not feasible in field environments. To that end, diagnostics pertaining to the state of the system, such as available power, communication reliability, and impedances to mobility could be made available to the user in order to monitor / manage system reliability [14].

The manner in which transparency is operationalized within a human–robot system evolves in parallel with the transition in robotics from tools to teammates. Looking toward the future, robots will no longer be expected to act as a conduit for telepresence; instead, robots will be expected to collaborate with humans in information-gathering and decision-making activities, as well as complement and extend the natural abilities of humans [15, 16]. Humans and robots may also be working together in task-based environments within the same physical space. As such, robotic platforms will require features that support a user’s understanding of what a system is doing or its functional status, as opposed to being invisible to the user. Likewise, the human user must be able to recognize and correctly interpret a robot’s transparency features as part of their overall situation awareness of a task environment. Understanding the status of a robot and what it is doing aids in the calibration and maintenance of trust in a robot’s reliability and ability to support the team in the successful completion of a given task.

The underlying, organizing framework for human understanding of robots is conceptualized as the mental model. Mental models are the mechanisms in users which facilitate system understanding, and are therefore critical to developing human– robot relationships. In the following section, we present a line of research examining the relationship between the visible behaviors of robots and human mental models regarding robots, and the influence of this relationship on transparency within the human–robot system.

## 2. MENTAL MODELS AND TRANSPARENCY

## 2.1. What are mental models?

Rouse and Morris [17] described mental models as “mechanisms whereby humans are able to generate descriptions of system purpose and form, explanations of system functioning and observed system states, and predictions of future states” (p. 7). The process of thinking through potential system outcomes based on the selection of inputs or actions has similarly been described as “experiments on an internal representation or model” (p. 8) [18]. However, mental models are applied to system interaction, regardless of their level of detail or accuracy [19]. Further, as models, they are an abstraction of reality, and are therefore not complete. Mental models are also malleable over time and can even be inaccurate to varying degrees. They are formed and influenced by previous experiences, superficial features of the target system, and even by analogs to other systems. However, this does not necessarily diminish the effectiveness of leveraging a mental model, depending upon the manner in which it is applied to a given system [20]. Simply stated, mental models act as a lens through which system behavior is perceived and interpreted [21].

For instance, motorists understand how to start an automobile and put it into motion. Driving an automobile is not an activity that requires intricate knowledge of how the sub-systems under the hood operate together to move the car forward; of course, some motorists understand the interaction of automobile sub-systems better than others. On the other hand, this level of knowledge of automobiles is required for a mechanic. Both motorists and mechanics maintain mental models of automobiles, but at different levels of detail. To that point, a signal of system transparency, such as the illumination of the check engine light, may provoke vastly different interpretations of the automobile’s system-state between the average motorist and automobile mechanic. Consider, then, how varying mental model representations of robotic systems may influence the interpretation and understanding of an autonomous robotic platform.

## 2.2. Interpretation of system intent

Prior research has demonstrated that humans readily attribute emotions and intentions to the motion behaviors of inanimate objects, including the classical study by Heider and Simmel [22] in which human observers interpreted the motions of two triangles and a circle, moving about a rectangular shape on a black and white screen. More recently, the interpretation and attribution of intent was also observed in interactions with automatic doors [23], automated home vacuum cleaning robots [24], an abstract single-appendage robot [25], as well as a prototypical unmanned ground vehicle [26]. However, these studies did not directly consider the influence of the mental model, in combination with the motion behavior of the system itself, on the interpretation of robotic system intent.

Someday in the near future, autonomous robots are expected to operate within urban environments. A significant factor for HRI which distinguishes the urban environment from other operational environments is that urban environments are populated with people that will potentially have very different mental models regarding the purpose and abilities of robots. We will assume that there will be a person designated as the robot handler (as opposed to an operator), who is primarily responsible for understanding how the robot functions within the task-environment. This person will likely have a highly detailed, accurate mental model of the autonomous robot. However, this is not the only person with whom a robot may interact, and we must also consider how other populations within the environment impact the ability of the human–robot team to complete a task. These other populations may include the handler’s immediate teammates, other teams within the same organization, teams from cooperating organizations (such as police and firefighters in disaster response), civilian bystanders, and even hostile forces. If transparency, then, were simply a characteristic of a robot, then it would follow that observers from each of these groups, presumably with different mental models, might interpret the actions of a robot similarly.

## 2.3. Interpretation of robot motion behavior

In order to examine this problem further, a basic research study was conducted to investigate the effects of mental models of inexperienced users of robots on the interpretation of robot motion behaviors, while controlling for a robot’s appearance and the environment in which the observation occurred. Specifically, participants were asked to observe the autonomous motion behaviors of a novel, yet plausible, robot platform within an outdoor park environment. The interaction occurred entirely within a simulated, virtual environment, using modified COTS software. The robot performed motion behaviors whose movement patterns were characteristic of either a security guard (e.g., patrolling, escorting, guarding) or a groundskeeper (e.g., mowing, organizing, cleaning). In order to simulate the effect of different mental models within population groups, participants were placed into one of three conditions: one group received preparatory information about the role and responsibilities of a prototypical security guard, one group received preparatory information about the role and responsibilities of a prototypical groundskeeper, and a third (control) group receiving no preparatory information. Each group of participants observed both sets of robot behaviors (security guard or groundskeeper, counterbalanced across groups). For each observed movement behavior, participants were asked to describe what the autonomous robot was trying to do, how sure they were of their interpretation, and were also asked to rate the robot on scales related to the following dimensions: intelligence, safety, power, and trustworthiness.

The results of the study supported the hypothesis that observers whose task-role mental models matched the role of the robot were significantly more accurate in correctly identifying the intent of the robot’s behavior. Also, under certain circumstances, having an incongruent mental model significantly hindered an observer’s ability to correctly interpret the robot’s intent; however, such observers were often just as sure of their inaccurate interpretations as the observers making accurate observations. Finally, positive associations were found within participants between differences in interpretation accuracy and subjective ratings of the robot along dimensions of intelligence, safety, and trust.

## 2.4. Impact of mental models and transparency within HRI

At a glance, these results may seem somewhat intuitive, however the results of this investigation suggested that transparency within a human–robot system could be improved without altering anything on the robot itself. Instead, the detail and accuracy of the mental models that humans bring into an interaction with a robot can influence the quality of the interaction. This is not to suggest that instructional design is a panacea for human–system design, because it is impossible to train every person who might possibly come into contact with an autonomous ground robot. The training information manipulation in this study was simply used as a means to simulate a potential real-world scenario (i.e., different mental models of what robots can do). In reality, humans that interact with a robot will apply some kind of mental model to understanding that robot, with varying degrees of success.

Therefore, in order to determine how to best support human–robot team transparency, it is important to know what the user knows about the robot, and robots in general. This information can be valuable for designing information-sharing features into robots that promote transparency among human teammates. Similarly, accounting for human mental models helps to potentially costly situations in which inaccurate interpretations, coupled with the certainty of the interpretations, lead to robot disuse or misplaced trust in the robot. The questions of how much and what type of information to be shared within the human–robot system in a mission environment are addressed in the following section, through the development of an agent transparency model.

## 3. SITUATION AWARENESS AND TRANSPARENCY

## 3.1. The SA-based Agent Transparency Model

Chen and colleagues defined agent transparency as a descriptive quality of an interface pertaining to its abilities to afford an operator’s comprehension about an intelligent agent’s intent, performance, future plans, and reasoning process [27]. Chen et al. propose a model of agent transparency to support operator situation awareness (SA) of the mission environment involving the agent — the SA-based Agent Transparency (SAT; Figure 1) — based on the theory of SA [28], the BDI (Beliefs, Desires, Intentions) Agent Framework [29], Agent’s 3P’s (purpose, process, and performance -- described below) [30], and other relevant previous work [27, 31-35]. According to Endsley [28], SA is “a state of knowledge” of “the state of a dynamic environment” (p. 36). It has three levels: (1) perception of basic elements, (2) comprehension of those elements’ meaning when taken as a whole, and (3) the ability to project the system’s status in the near-term based on that comprehension. Based on Endsley’s SA model, the SAT model attempts to identify features of the environment necessary for the operator’s global SA involving the agent(s). Endsley’s model refers to cognitive requirements for different levels of global SA, whereas the SAT model refers to transparency requirements to understand the intelligent agent’s task parameters, logic, and predicted outcomes.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 1. SA-based Agent Transparency Model.

The SAT model also incorporates Agent’s 3 P’s (Purpose, Process, and Performance), which has been identified as an antecedent for trust development in the context of human-agent interaction [30]. The Purpose factor deals with the degree to which the agent-driven automation is being used according to the designer’s intent. The Process factor deals with the question of whether the algorithm of the automated system is appropriate for a given task. The Performance factor deals with system reliability, predictability, and capability. Lee [36] proposed that, in order to increase system transparency to the operator, the system’s 3P’s as well as the history of the 3P’s should be visible to the operator.

Finally, the SAT model addresses the issues of informing the operator about the agent’s Beliefs, Desires, and Intentions (BDI) [29]. The BDI framework has been used to develop mixed-initiative systems in various contexts, where agents’ beliefs are updated based on their perception of the environment, communications with other agents/humans, and their inference mechanisms [29, 37, 38]. Once the agent’s beliefs are updated and if new tasks are identified, the agent continues with goal-selection (Desires), and planning/execution (Intentions). In order for the agent to be optimally transparent to the human operator, its Beliefs-Desires-Intentions need to be effectively conveyed to the human when appropriate. Conveying the agent’s BDI to the human operator should, in theory, benefit the human-agent team’s shared mental model and therefore human-agent teaming, although empirical evidence is still lacking to establish that connection [35, 39].

## 3.2. Applying the SAT Model to User Interface Designs

At the first level of the SAT model, the operator is provided with the basic information about the agent’s current state, goals, intentions, and proposed actions. At the second level, the operator is provided with information about the agent’s reasoning process behind those actions and the constraints/affordances that the agent considers when planning the actions. At the third level, the operator is provided with information regarding the agent’s projection of the future state, such as predicted consequences, likelihood of success/failure, and any uncertainty associated with the above. Incorporating all three levels should allow an operator to gain understanding of an agent’s reasoning process behind its actions and help the operator make informed decisions as to whether he or she should intervene. Additionally, the SAT model differs from Endsley’s [28] SA model in that not all three levels may be absolutely necessary to achieving transparency — they are simply different aspects. In Endsley’s model, SA is the cumulative result of the levels, while transparency may not be. For example, in a time-sensitive situation, the operator may only need to know the agent’s proposed actions (Level 1) and the projected outcome (Level 3) to make a sufficiently-informed decision.

It is important that agent transparency information be presented in a simplified form (e.g., integrated graphical displays), so the operator is not overwhelmed by the volume of information that they need to process [40, 41]. Miller [42] cautioned interface designers’ attempts to achieve “full transparency,” which can increase the operator’s workload and reduce the utility of the automation. Information visualization strategies such as the Ecological Interface Designs (EID) can potentially be useful for conveying agent transparency information [43].

The effectiveness of EIDs for human-agent interaction has been investigated in several studies [44-47]. In these studies, EIDs have been used to graphically portray the capabilities and limitations of agent, intent of agent, and quality of plan revisions proposed by agent. These studies consistently found that EIDs were effective in supporting both operators’ understandings of agents’ behavior as well as their predictions of agents’ future behaviors, thereby promoting proper operator trust calibration. We expand upon the discussion of trust in the following section.

## 4. TRUST AND TRANSPARENCY

Transparency is often referred to in definitions of trust as a desirable, possibly even necessary, component [48]. And, similar to transparency, trust is an emergent property that is created through the interaction between two entities [49]. General trust is often described as a belief that someone or something will be honest and reliable [50], or, as a willingness to be vulnerable [51]; this is indeed descriptive of human-automation and human-robot interaction (HAI and HRI) as well. Lee and See [30] described trust as “the attitude that an agent will help achieve an individual’s goals in a situation characterized by uncertainty and vulnerability” (p. 54).

Due to the relative nascency of the field of robotics, there have been few articles published on trust in this domain until recently. Fortunately, since robots are complex automated systems, the study of trust in automation informs this developing arena. Particularly applicable here is the work in trust calibration and appropriate use. When a user trusts a system too much, this can lead to misuse, which leads to over-reliance on a system. Misuse may occur when users trust the automation more than their own or their teammates’ capabilities, and is more probable when automation is highly reliable. Examples of misuse are automation-induced complacency and automation bias, said to affect automation under supervisory control and decision aids respectively [52]. Conversely, too little trust in a system leads to disuse - ignoring or turning off features inappropriately, under-utilization, or even complete lack of use [53]. Moray and Inagaki [54] referred to such low-trust behavior as “skeptical.” This behavior leads an operator to over-monitor, and potentially make more errors due to neglect of other systems. Therefore, it is crucial to appropriate utilization practices that user trust be properly calibrated [30]. Indeed, trust is a critical factor in determining whether to even use an automation [55].

While robots are complex automated devices, there are key differences between robotic systems and other automated systems. Robots generally exhibit features such as mobility, anthropomorphism, and the ability to effect action at a distance [49]. However, just as with other automated systems, trust calibration is key to appropriate usage. Since trust is an emergent property of the interaction, proper trust calibration cannot occur by adjustment to robot features alone. It is not the features and behaviors of the robot that are mediating trust – rather, it is the user’s perception of these features and behaviors. Through the use of robotics, human limitations (sensory, psychomotor, cognitive) can be can be ameliorated, and human capabilities extended [56]. But to best do this, systems must behave in a manner that supports human needs and expectations [57, 58].

## 4.1. Factors that influence trust

Hancock and colleagues [49] investigated the factors that influence trust in HRI through a meta-analysis. This research revealed three main categories of antecedents: human-related, robot-related, and environmental (see Figure 2). Robotrelated factors such as behavior, reliability, and predictability were shown to be highly related to trust. Environmental factors, including elements of the situation such as task type and communication between the human and robot, were also moderately related. Interestingly, factors associated with the human user, such as prior experience, attention capacity, personality, and demographics were not related in the meta-analysis; however, the authors pointed out that this may have been due to a lack of previous research measuring these constructs in terms of human–robot interaction. Certainly, factors such as propensity to trust are integral to any type of trust relationship [59].

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 2: Antecedents of trust in HRI

Definitions of trust often mention reliability [30, 60], and indeed, the authors of the above meta-analysis stated that overall trends in current literature associated higher trust with higher reliability [49]. Similarly, a review by Merritt and Ilgen [59] reported that such factors as consistency, dependability, performance, predictability, and reliability — all robot-related features — influence trust.

While robot-related features are important to the trust relationship, human-related features must be considered equally in order to fully understand the interaction. Research on individual differences in trust in HRI has explored how differences in user characteristics influence these interactions. These differences may be highly influential on trust. In one study, researchers found that the individual differences of dispositional trust and propensity to trust machines accounted for 52% of the trust variance above the effects of actual characteristics [59].

However, a high propensity to trust can sometimes exacerbate the negative effects of malfunction on trust because hightrust operators have greater expectations for machine performance [59], so they may not be monitoring the automation as closely as they otherwise would when the malfunction occurs. However, this interaction between high trust and malfunction may also reflect a greater sensitivity to system performance in high trust individuals for both good and bad [30]. For example, Singh, Molloy, and Parasuraman [61] found that participants whom they categorized as “high complacency” actually displayed superior performance on error detection in a constant-reliability condition. This can be explained by studies on trust in human social interaction, which showed that trusting individuals assign trust more appropriately than less trusting individuals [30].

Just as a user’s perception of the efficacy of a robotic counterpart is crucial to the trust relationship, so is their perception of their own efficacy or confidence. If a user is confident that he has the capability to perform a given task himself, he may choose to maintain manual control and may not develop trust in a robot or other automated aid, whereas those with lower self-confidence may trust and rely on the robot more readily [62, 63]. Lee and Moray [63] found that users switch to manual control when their self-confidence supersedes their trust in the automation and, conversely, use automation when trust supersedes self-confidence.

Since trust is an emergent construct depending on the interaction between the human and the robot, the environment in which that interaction takes place is also important. Cultural factors such as power distance, uncertainty avoidance, and individualism/collectivism influence cultural variations in trust [64, 65]. Furthermore, HRI is improved when robots exhibit behavior culturally-prescribed by the human with which they interact, such as the utilization of increased implicit communication in high-context cultures [58, 65].

## 4.2. Human–robot teams

In the past, robots have often been thought of as simple tools, capable of little more than teleoperation, but current systems are designed with the expectation that robots will be fully integrated into mixed human-robot teams as team members [49]. Here, the human-robot team becomes a system, and for the system to function appropriately, trust must be appropriately calibrated. User characteristics such as knowledge (i.e., mental models), skills, abilities and attitudes should be considered when assembling human-robot teams [66]. Another important facet of this type of team dynamic is the amount of experience the user has had with the robot. The more a human user interacts with an automated system, the more the user will trust it [30].

As true human–automation teams develop in place of the traditional low-automation supervisory control relationship, the goal of designing for transparency will increasingly progress from making the interface “invisible” to users [67] to enhancing the amount and quality of communication between robot and human. Increased transparency will lead to improved trust and performance outcomes.

## 4.3. Trust and transparency in HRI

As previously mentioned, trust must be properly calibrated in order to achieve appropriate usage of any type of automated system. Transparency supports this calibration by ensuring that the expectations of the user are based on the appropriate foundations. Trust in a robot is not necessarily based on what that robot is capable of; rather, trust is based on what the user perceives the robot’s capabilities to be. This is an important distinction, because perception and reality are not always the same thing, as demonstrated by the mental model study described in the previous section.

Our current work investigates transparency factors that may influence human trust in a robotic teammate, and the effect of robot malfunction on this relationship through two ongoing experiments. In Experiment 1, we are examining the effects of varying levels of information (LOI) provided to a participant by a robotic teammate upon the participant’s trust and workload, as well as the influence of the modality of communication (auditory, graphic, or video). Partial results of this work may be found in Sanders et al. [68]. In Experiment 2, which is also ongoing, we are again varying LOI and modality and measuring trust workload, but this experiment also includes a malfunction condition wherein the communication between the participant and the robot takes place during incidents of malfunction. Through this line of experimentation, we hope to increase understanding of transparency to support trust calibration, and ultimately appropriate utilization of robotic teammates.

## 5. CONCLUSION

Looking toward the future, transparency within human–robot teams will continue to be vital as robots transition from teleoperated tools to collaborating teammates. However, the operationalization of transparency in human–robot systems will also transition from invisibility to understandability as robots become more autonomous, operating within populated environments and supporting human teammates in physical and cognitive task elements. In this document, we described three interdisciplinary efforts to examine the role of transparency in continuously-evolving HRI relationships, and the relevance of transparency to other HRI-critical constructs including mental models, situation awareness and trust. Specifically, mental models represent the underlying, organizing framework for human understanding of robots, serving as the lens through which humans interpret and reason about a robot’s actions, abilities, and usefulness. Thus, mental models provide for the activation of situation awareness in humans. The SA-based Agent Transparency Model outlines the type of information that can be conveyed within a user interface to promote situation awareness during agent interaction. Supporting the development of SA within a human teammate through the implementation of transparency features is one way in which trust can be calibrated in HRI. The proper calibration of trust helps to ensure that robot teammates are leveraged effectively in dynamic task environments, such as urban operations.

This is easier described than implemented, however. The research presented here also called attention to potential pitfalls in the implementation of transparency. Human mental models regarding robots can be incomplete or inaccurate, which may lead to the misunderstanding of agent transparency information, or an unawareness of the information altogether. Agent transparency features, intended to support human situation awareness, may be uninformative or overwhelming to a user, thus diminishing their effectiveness. Further, trust in autonomous systems is something which must be calibrated, meaning that it is a moving target. Too much trust in a system may lead to overreliance, while a lack of trust may result in a disregard for the system. Finally, transparency is just one of many factors (see Figure 2) that can influence trust in robots.

In HRI, mental models, situation awareness, and trust all interact with transparency and with one another. As such, with respect to human–robot teams, system transparency is not simply a characteristic or list of features associated with a robotic hardware, software, or interface, but a product of team interaction. There will likely be best practices that emerge in the development of robotics that can offer the greatest transparency for the greatest number of people. However, transparency is achieved when a human can recognize (i.e., situation awareness) and accurately interpret (i.e., mental models) information from a robot, and then properly trust in that information to make actionable decisions to leverage a robot in an operational environment. Therefore, we identify system transparency as an emergent property of the human–robot system. Finally, just as system transparency is achieved within the collaboration of human and robot teammates, identifying best practices for transparency is an interdisciplinary effort that requires collaboration between scientists, engineers, designers, and users. Hopefully, the information presented here will continue the dialog and collaboration across institutions and disciplines toward the long-term development of human–robot teamwork.
